Leela, you asked if I tell my parents everything. No. My poems are mine. How I feel about my cousin's wedding drama is mine. That's just private, like a room with a door.
But last month there was something else. A senior kept messaging me, saying he'd post an edited photo of me if I didn't do his project. I hid it from everyone. I told myself it was private too. It wasn't. Private is my poems. That was a secret keeping me in danger.
So on Friday I showed my aunt the messages. She didn't panic. She took screenshots, sat with me and said, "Dilnaz, you did right to tell me. This isn't your fault." She rang the school that same afternoon, and the principal called his parents in on Monday.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's aunt do that same afternoon?
qa.a: She rang the school that same afternoon.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel while hiding the messages, and what did Dilnaz come to see?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt scared while hiding them, and came to see they were not private like the poems but a secret keeping Dilnaz in danger.

qa.q: Why was showing the aunt the messages the right step?
qa.a: It brought in an adult who could act: she took screenshots, reassured Dilnaz and contacted the school the same day.

qa.q: How might Leela understand the difference between private and secret after this story?
qa.a: Leela might see that keeping poems and feelings to yourself is healthy, but hiding threats only protects the person causing harm.

grounding: A teenager explains that poems and feelings are ordinary privacy, while hiding threatening messages was secrecy that protected danger.

I'm Seema, Saurabh's didi. Since he turned fifteen, my brother has become a closed door. He writes in a notebook he takes everywhere, texts someone and smiles, won't say who. Mummy worries. I don't, much; I was fifteen once, and I kept a notebook too.
But Wednesday was different. He came home with his sleeve pulled over his wrist in the heat, and flinched when I bumped his arm. He said he'd fallen. He wouldn't look at me.
I sat down with him on the stairs and said, "Your notebook is yours. This isn't the same. Did someone hurt you?" After a long time he nodded: some older boys at the bus stop. I told him it wasn't his fault. We told Mummy together that evening, and she called the school straight away.

qa.q: What did Saurabh say had happened to his arm?
qa.a: He said he'd fallen.

qa.q: What does Seema think about Saurabh's notebook and smiling at texts?
qa.a: She thinks it's ordinary privacy, remembering she kept a notebook at fifteen too, so she isn't worried by it.

qa.q: What did Seema do that helped once she noticed the wrist?
qa.a: She sat with him, separated his private notebook from the injury, asked directly, said it wasn't his fault, and told Mummy with him that evening.

qa.q: What might Saurabh have been feeling when he pulled his sleeve down and wouldn't look at Seema?
qa.a: He was probably scared and ashamed, trying to hide the harm, and may have worried that telling would make things worse.

grounding: An older sister sees her brother's notebook as healthy privacy but recognises that hiding an injury is secrecy, and gets help that day.

Rafiq kept his poetry notebook under his mattress, and when his sister Himani teased him about it, he just smiled. That was his. Nobody needed to read his poems about the river and the girl who sold flowers at the bus stand.
But the other thing was different.
For a week, two older boys from the next village had been waiting near the canal. "Carry this packet to the highway dhaba," they said, pushing money at him. "Don't tell your family. Easy money."
Rafiq noticed the difference in his own stomach. The notebook he kept private because it was precious. This he was hiding because he was scared.
That evening, he found his Chacha fixing the tractor. He told him everything. His Chacha put down the spanner. "You did right. You won't go near them again. Tonight I'll speak to the sarpanch, and tomorrow I'll walk you to school."

qa.q: Where did Rafiq keep his poetry notebook?
qa.a: Under his mattress.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel about the packets, compared with his notebook?
qa.a: Rafiq noticed he felt calm keeping the notebook private but scared and uneasy about hiding the packets, which told him the two were different.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's Chacha do after hearing about the packets?
qa.a: He told Rafiq he did right, said he'd speak to the sarpanch that night, and promised to walk him to school the next day.

qa.q: How does Himani see Rafiq's notebook?
qa.a: Himani sees it as something fun to tease him about, while Rafiq sees it as precious and private.

grounding: It shows a teenager keeping his poems private for dignity while recognising that hiding contact with older boys protects danger, and telling an adult.

passage:
In Cape Town, Oskar kept a journal on his desk that his mother never opened, and a playlist he never let his older brother see. Private, not hidden. His parents knew about it and left it alone.
On Friday, Lindiwe, his friend from the swim team, messaged the group: "Quarry tonight at midnight. Jumping off the top ledge. Nobody tells their parents."
Oskar stared at his screen. The journal was his to keep. But this was something else. He knew someone had broken both legs at that quarry last year.
He messaged Lindiwe privately: "I'm not coming, and I'm going to tell my dad. I don't want you getting hurt."
Then he went downstairs. His father listened, then called Lindiwe's mother and two other parents straight away. By ten, the plan had fallen apart.
Lindiwe didn't message him for days. But she didn't jump either.

qa.q: When was the quarry jump planned?
qa.a: Tonight at midnight.

qa.q: How did Oskar feel when he saw the group message?
qa.a: Oskar felt alarmed and worried for Lindiwe, knowing this secret was about danger, unlike his journal.

qa.q: What did Oskar and his father do to keep the group safe?
qa.a: Oskar told Lindiwe he would tell, then told his father, who called Lindiwe's mother and other parents straight away.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe see Oskar's choice?
qa.a: Lindiwe may feel angry or betrayed at first, not messaging Oskar for days, but Lindiwe stayed safe because of it.

grounding: It shows a teenager distinguishing his private journal from a group secret that protects danger, and telling a trusted adult the same evening.

In the counsellor's room at school, Rashmi sat with her hands in her lap. Ms Rajni had asked the class to write about "private and secret" for health class, and Rashmi had stayed back.
"I keep lots of things to myself," Rashmi said. "Like my poems. Or that I miss my old school. That's just private, right?"
"Right. That's yours," Ms Rajni said.
"But there's one other thing. A college boy on a game server. He says we're special friends. He says I shouldn't tell anyone because they wouldn't get it." Rashmi looked at the floor. "That one feels different. Like I'm hiding it, not just keeping it."
Ms Rajni's voice stayed calm. "You're right. That's a secret that protects him, not you. Thank you for telling me. This isn't your fault." She moved her chair closer. "Let's block him together now, and I'll call your mother this afternoon so we can decide the next step with her."
Rashmi nodded, shaky but lighter.

qa.q: What does the college boy tell Rashmi?
qa.a: He says they're special friends and that she shouldn't tell anyone because they wouldn't get it.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel about the game-server secret?
qa.a: Rashmi felt uneasy and ashamed, sensing it was hiding rather than just keeping something private.

qa.q: What did Ms Rajni do that same day?
qa.a: Stayed calm, said it wasn't Rashmi's fault, blocked the contact with her, and planned to call Rashmi's mother that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's mother be affected by the call?
qa.a: Her mother would likely feel worried but grateful that Rashmi spoke up and that the school acted the same day.
